narrative:
The model determined that you have a 56.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Being in the second decile means you placed in the bottom 20% of your class that year, well below the average of roughly the sixth decile among students who were accepted. This low ranking signaled to the model a higher risk that you would struggle with the bar exam.

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and worked in the opposite direction. At 39, your score sits slightly above the 37.2 average of accepted students, which helped pull the prediction back toward passing. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.10 was the third most influential feature. Although the effect was smaller, it still nudged the outcome slightly toward failure because it falls a bit below the 3.23 average of admitted applicants.

Taken together, the model concluded that your academic performance in law school, especially the weak third-year ranking, outweighed the positive signal from your LSAT.

What you should do next is straightforward: focus on strengthening your academic record and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score further. Improving your class rank in future years or completing targeted bar-preparation coursework could also shift future predictions in your favor. Many students successfully reapply after addressing exactly these areas.
